summary: Specifies the MPLS Transport Profile data plane, meaning how packets are encapsulated and forwarded inside an MPLS-TP network. It is a joint IETF and ITU-T effort. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: The rules for how packages are wrapped and moved along the roads of a transport network.

subtitle: The data plane of MPLS-TP: how packets are labelled and forwarded over transport paths, pseudowires and sections.

tldr.problem: Packet-switched transport networks need an MPLS data plane that meets transport requirements, as part of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS-TP reuses the ordinary MPLS and pseudowire data planes and adds a few rules, such as no ECMP, penultimate hop popping off by default, and a Generic Associated Channel for OAM traffic.
tldr.outcome: It names the data plane functions of MPLS-TP and says which an implementation must support. RFC 7274 later updated it.

facts.label: ECMP
facts.value: MUST NOT be performed on an MPLS-TP LSP

today: RFC 5960 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7274. The data plane rules described here remain a base for MPLS-TP.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is the set of MPLS functions for building and running packet-switched transport networks. RFC 5960 specifies the data plane: the layer that handles encapsulation and forwarding of packets. It builds on the MPLS data plane of RFC 3031 and RFC 3032 and the pseudowire architecture of RFC 3985, and the overall architecture is in RFC 5921.

The document has two goals: to identify the data plane functions of MPLS-TP, and to say which of them an implementation is required to support. It covers packets traversing an MPLS-TP label switched path (LSP), pseudowire (PW) or section. How packets get into or out of those entities is out of scope. It is a product of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort.
sections.eli5: This is the rulebook for how wagons are tagged and moved on the track, not for how they get onto the track.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Forwarding
sections.content:
MPLS-TP forwarding follows the standard MPLS data plane, plus the single-segment and multi-segment pseudowire architectures, except where this document says otherwise. An MPLS-TP packet has a label stack, and the usual push, pop and swap operations apply. The stack represents a hierarchy of LSPs: pushing a label adds a level and popping removes it.

Unlike general MPLS, support for IP host and router functions on MPLS-TP interfaces is OPTIONAL. Forwarding is based on the label that identifies an LSP or PW, and a swap treats the rest of the packet as opaque. The only event that interrupts a swap is TTL expiry. When that happens, the bottom-of-stack label is inspected, and if it is a reserved label such as the G-ACh Label, the packet is handled by that label's rules. For a pseudowire, the packet is checked for an Associated Channel Header below the PW label.
sections.eli5: A station only reads the tag on the outside and swaps it for a new one. It only opens the wagon if the tag has timed out.

sections.title: Label Switched Paths
sections.content:
MPLS-TP LSPs are ordinary MPLS LSPs unless noted. Quality of service comes from Traffic Engineered LSPs and MPLS Diffserv, and both E-LSP and L-LSP modes are included. The Traffic Class field is processed according to RFC 5462 and RFC 3270. The Uniform, Pipe and Short Pipe tunneling models MAY be used, but Pipe or Short Pipe support is REQUIRED for typical transport applications.

Several rules are specific to MPLS-TP. ECMP load-balancing MUST NOT be performed on an MPLS-TP LSP, though a server layer may load-balance transparently. Penultimate Hop Popping MUST be disabled by default. LSP payloads are network-layer packets or pseudowire packets, and the label stack is contiguous with the payload's stack, with exactly one label entry having the S bit set to 1.

Four LSP types are included: point-to-point unidirectional, point-to-point associated bidirectional, point-to-point co-routed bidirectional, and point-to-multipoint unidirectional.
sections.eli5: Some roads are one-way, some are two-way, and some send copies to many places. Traffic is not split over parallel roads, so it arrives in order.

sections.title: Sections and Pseudowires
sections.content:
A section is the connectivity between two topologically adjacent MPLS-TP LSRs at a layer: a data link at layer 0 or an LSP above that. The links traversed by a layer n+1 LSP are layer n sections, so the LSP is a client and the section layer is its server. A section may offer point-to-point bidirectional, point-to-point unidirectional or point-to-multipoint unidirectional service. It MUST provide a way to identify the type of payload it carries.

Pseudowires follow the existing single-segment (RFC 3985) and multi-segment architectures. The RFC lists example PW encapsulations, such as Ethernet over MPLS and structure-agnostic TDM, and states that it specifies no modifications or extensions to pseudowire data plane architectures or protocols.
sections.eli5: A section is one stretch of track between two stations. A pseudowire is a sealed pipe that carries someone else's traffic inside.

sections.title: The Generic Associated Channel
sections.content:
The Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), from RFC 5586, is an auxiliary channel for sections, LSPs and PWs. Its main purpose is control, management and OAM traffic. It MUST NOT carry client layer network traffic.

On a pseudowire, the first four bits after the bottom-of-stack label discriminate: a value of 1 marks a G-ACh packet, and the next 32 bits form the Associated Channel Header (ACH), which says what kind of traffic it is. On a section or LSP, a reserved label with value 13, the G-ACh Label (GAL), sits at the bottom of the label stack and signals that the payload begins with an ACH. Data plane implementations MUST give the application enough context, such as the receiving interface or received label stack, to process a G-ACh packet.
sections.eli5: It is a special lane for service messages. A special tag at the bottom says that this wagon is for the staff and not a customer.

sections.title: Server-Layer Considerations
sections.content: MPLS-TP needs nothing from the server layer beyond the type of service its transport entities require, and has no awareness of the server's internals. What looks like one server-layer link may be a complicated construct such as an LSP or a bundle of links, and special care may be needed then. How MPLS-TP packets are encapsulated for specific server-layer media is outside this document.
sections.eli5: The network does not care what is under the track, only that the train can run on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MPLS data plane, and so the MPLS-TP data plane, provides no security mechanisms of its own. Client layers that want to protect their data are REQUIRED to apply their own. Control or management protocols that install label operations are equipped with security features operators can use.

Where a trust relationship exists with a peer, an LSR MAY discard any received MPLS packet unless every label processed at the receiver was a value the receiver distributed to that neighbor, or one previously distributed to the peer beyond that neighbor. Further detail is in RFC 5921 and RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: The tags have no lock, so people who want secret cargo must lock it themselves. A station can also ignore wagons with tags it never handed out.

items.title: P2P unidirectional
items.text: Supported by basic MPLS and works the same way in MPLS-TP.

items.title: P2P associated bidirectional
items.text: Two unidirectional LSPs, one each way, treated as a pair.

items.title: P2P co-routed bidirectional
items.text: An associated pair that follows the same nodes and links, so the two LSPs share fate.

items.title: P2MP unidirectional
items.text: Same label processing as P2P, but a packet is sent out all associated egress interfaces.
